reason: Raised by 6 to put this repository's schema under the shared migration ledger (internal/pgmigrate). It was one of two schemas in the product and the other is the reconciliation store; leaving this one applied as an unversioned blob on every start, to protect a line count, would be optimising the metric over the thing the metric is a proxy for. The rule is NOT here. The ledger table, the advisory lock that keeps two replicas from racing the DDL, the once-only application and the transaction that commits a migration together with the row recording it are all in internal/pgmigrate, which is 200 lines and imports nothing of this context's. What lands in controlplane is six lines: the import, a two-line comment saying where the mechanism lives, and the three that turn the existing const into a named migration. None of it can move -- conduit_repository_state and conduit_repository_blobs are this context's tables and their DDL goes wherever they go. The schema text itself is unchanged, character for character. Adoption is safe because every statement in it is already conditional -- two CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS and one INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, no ALTER, nothing destructive -- so the first start after this change runs it once more against a populated database and does nothing, then records it. This raise should come back down when these tables are displaced into a bounded context: the migration moves with them and the six lines leave with it. The previous 24937 was recorded on 2026-08-17 and read: Raised by 64 to name the conflict between an intermittent Environment and an evidence-age bound (#65, second gap). An Environment declared INTERMITTENT_AGENTS reports when it next connects, so its health is honestly 'as of last connection'; any MaximumEvidenceAgeSeconds shorter than that cadence refuses it. The refusal was correct and its sentence was not: 'stale health evidence' is what an outage reads like, and it sent operators to investigate an Environment behaving exactly as configured. The bound is NOT exempted, which was the stated constraint and is also the only design the code permits. EVIDENCE_STALE is still derived and still blocks; the new ENVIRONMENT_EVIDENCE_BOUND_CONFLICT accompanies it. That is what makes it replay-safe: validatePromotions has no repository and can never re-derive an Environment-dependent blocker, so it takes those on trust precisely because they only ever make a promotion fail to pass. A blocker that relaxed anything could not be trusted on the same terms, and a record that passed on excused evidence would fail to reproduce. The rule is NOT here. The age comparison went to internal/catalog/domain as EvidenceExceedsAgeBound, exported so ValidateEvidence and this caller ask the same question rather than keeping two copies that drift; the blocker kind is a catalog constant. What lands in controlplane is intermittentEvidenceBoundConflicts, which resolves each evidence Environment's federation and cannot leave: it needs the Repository and a context, which the catalog domain deliberately has neither of, and it is the exact shape of nonParticipatingEvidenceEnvironments beside it. Most of the 64 is comment: why the bound is not waived, why additive-only is what buys replay trust, and why the message names both halves of the disagreement -- naming only the Environment reads as a fault, naming only the policy reads as a misconfiguration, and it is the pair that is wrong. Four mutations killed, including waiving the bound, raising the conflict for fresh evidence, raising it for continuously-reporting Environments, and dropping the replay trust. The previous 24873 was recorded on 2026-08-17 and read: Raised by 17 to let an errored Change Request be reopened (#56). A crq_ id is derived from its target alone, so whatever record a target carries first it carries for good -- every later proposal collides and receives the stored one back. ERROR was the worst status to be stuck in and the only one Reopen refused: it is not a decision anybody took, since evaluateChangeRequest writes it when a policy fails to evaluate, when every policy returns no_op, or when no policy is enabled at all. So a deployment that proposed anything before configuring its approval policies burnt that target permanently, with no recourse open to any principal -- not even the author, who is the only principal Reopen admits. The change is one clause in the status gate; the rest is the comment recording why ERROR is admitted beside two decisions without being one, and that reopening re-evaluates against the policies in force now, so a still-broken configuration errors again and costs nothing. This cannot move to a bounded context: Reopen is the Change Request lifecycle, which internal/governance/domain explicitly disclaims at change.go -- the record 'belongs to the context that owns the request's lifecycle'. The same reasoning as the #55 and #56 entries below. Deliberately not included: carrying the prior Reviews forward, which an adversarial review recommended in the same breath. Reopen rebuilds the record without them, so a rejection's rationale -- the only durable copy, since the audit event records who and when but reasons the success as 'authorized' -- is destroyed on reopen. That is a real defect, and the recommended fix interacts: approveOnce refuses a principal who already appears in Reviews, so carrying a rejection forward would permanently bar the rejecting reviewer from approving the revised request. It needs its own design and is filed rather than guessed at. The previous 24856 was recorded on 2026-08-17 and read: Raised by 88 to stop an approved Change Request being replayed as a standing pre-approval (#56). A crq_ id is a digest of TargetKind and TargetID alone, so a second proposal against the same target collides and CreateChangeRequest returns the record already stored; the evaluation this call performed is discarded. Every handler that auto-applied on Status == APPROVED therefore performed the action again under whatever policy is in force now -- reproduced here at the export-pipeline routes and, worse, on the deployment path, where supersedePendingPlans cancels an approved Plan without touching its Change Request, so re-proposing superseded desired state resurrected a CANCELLED Plan to APPROVED and cleared its cancellation while the policy rejected the identical proposal on fresh state. Two further routes reached the same side effect without proposing at all: PUT /v1/change-requests/{id}/labels takes no decision, leaves an already-satisfied record APPROVED, and its handler re-ran the pipeline action. The predicate is the current verdict, not "did this call create the record": creation was the first design and an adversarial review killed it, which a test in this commit records -- archive, unarchive, archive again is an ordinary sequence whose second archive collides, and gating on creation refused it under a policy that had not changed, with no route left that could perform it. None of this can move to a bounded context. internal/governance/domain deliberately holds ChangeFacts rather than the request record, saying so at change.go: the record "belongs to the context that owns the request's lifecycle", which is this one -- as is the repository whose collision creates the problem, the mux, and finalizeApprovedChangeRequest. The same reasoning the #55 entry below records. Roughly two thirds of the 88 is comment: why the verdict is read before CreateChangeRequest rather than after, why Approve and Reopen may apply while Reject, Cancel and Labels may not (Reopen re-evaluates against the policy in force, so its APPROVED is a decision taken now), and the record of the reversed design so it is not proposed again. Honest limits: three of the five proposal sites are additionally protected today by an incidental property -- a revision CAS in Prepare, a content-derived TargetID, a status check in LinkImportChangeRequest -- so the guard there is defence in depth and a mutation removing it alone survives the suite; the fleet site likewise, because its execution record already refuses a second successful run. The terminal-record wedge that is the other half of #56 is untouched and still blocked on a product decision.
